messages.author: c09cdb35cca40b8e
messages.subject: geom_jitter()
parts:
Dear ggplot2 group

I am working at a pharmaceutical company and am moving the data visualisation component from a variety of methods to the ggplot2 framework.

I am a little surprised to find something a little strange with geom_jitter(). In my department a boxplot with jittered data points is rather critical plot for many analyses so that the distributions of data points underlying the plot can be questioned.

Let us consider the following code

library(ggplot2)
data <- cbind(as.data.frame(cbind(NULL, rep(LETTERS[1:8],8))),rnorm(64))
colnames(data) <- c("class", "signal")
print(ggplot(data, aes(class, signal)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter())

I create a data.frame with 8 "experimental classes", each of which has 8 measurements.
This is plotted as a boxplot with jitter. Everything looks pretty OK. However when I run the code one of the classes often has more jittered dots than it has observations within the data. In most graphs there is at least one class with 9 dots, in some cases a column with 10 data points is seen.

Does anyone else see this problem? Is there something fundamentally stupid that I am doing. I have checked several times and it is not just the case that I can't count! This is seen using both OSX ggplot2_0.8.5 and 64bit linux with ggplot2_0.8.7.

Thanks, greetings from Finland

Stephen

messages.author: 936ef8c6d12fc338
messages.subject: RE: geom_jitter()
parts:
Dear Stephen,

Notice that you plot your data twice: once as a boxplots and once as a
jitter plot. Suppose you have 9 observations of which one is an outlier.
The boxplot will display that outliers as a point. The jitter geom plots
a point for each observation. Hence you end up with 10 points (9 from
jitter, 1 from boxplot). Try putting the jitter points in a different
color or shape. Then you'll see the difference.

HTH,

Thierry

PS Boxplots might not be a very good idea if you have only 9
observations...
